newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury refunding ends, demand seen mediocre.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury refunding ends, demand seen mediocre.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury raised $39.75 billion as it ended its quarterly refunding Thursday to sell securities to fund government operations.
But Wall Street experts said demand at the three-day auction was mediocre, with the largest purchases by foreign central banks and Wall Street dealers.

"I'd say that all three auctions were average," said Jerry Zukowski, money market economist at PaineWebber. "It'll get done, but it's certainly less than exciting in terms of the levels at which these things were taken down."

The Treasury ended the refunding Thursday, placing $10.0 billion in fresh 30-year bonds at an average yield of 6.640 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio -- the number of bids received compared with the number of bids accepted -- was 2.42 to one, the highest for this refunding.
The government placed $12.0 billion of 10-year notes Wednesday at an average yield of 6.374 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio was a low 1.90 to one.
On Tuesday, the Treasury sold $17.754 billion in three-year notes at an average yield of 5.997 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio in the auction was 2.22 to one.
Analysts said they noticed some hedge and pension funds bidding for the longer-dated maturities, but portfolio managers were seen as mostly sidelined.
Retail brokerages were the big no-show at the refunding.
"Most retail shops didn't show up at all at the auctions. This refunding was mostly led by professional and some institutional players," the trader added.

Some players expressed concern that the Wall Street dealer community might be holding more paper than it would like, which could prompt some delayed selling down the road that would depress overall prices.
"We might see some downward pressure on prices here as people unload these new papers," said a trader at foreign investment bank here.

Some analysts, however, were optimistic about the Treasury market's short-term outlook. "The paper will get distributed over the next couple of days ... But there is enough demand for that," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist of fixed-income at Credit Suisse First Boston.

Analysts said a combination of factors, ranging from concerns about the future performance of the dollar to a large requirement of fresh cash, discouraged many players from aggressively bidding at the refunding auctions.

Recent comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin saying the dollar has been strong "for some time" cast doubt on the future of the dollar and, as a result, poured cold water on investors' appetite for the new securities.
Analysts said buyers remained edgy even though the dollar has remained firm against most major currencies, including the German mark and Japanese yen.
"The uncertainty about the dollar took some of the luster out of these refunding auctions," the trader at the foreign investment bank said.
Traders said the Treasury raised a sizable amount of new cash at the refunding given the large amount of new issuance. But, they noted, there were not a lot of securities maturing.

Market experts estimated that out of a total of $39.75 billion in securities being sold at the refunding, nearly $21.0 billion was bought with funds that had not been rolled over from older securities that had matured.
